findings.title: animate=True/'window' with continuous (per-observation) hue silently loses the animation: full trajectory drawn statically, window/trails never shown
findings.description: When hue= is a per-observation numeric array (multicolor-line path), plot.py's _apply_multicolor_lines (plot.py:3249) runs AFTER the animation is built and does `for line in list(ax.lines): line.remove()` -- removing the very Line3D artists update_lines_parallel drives each frame -- then adds the FULL trajectory as a static Line3DCollection. Every frame of the exported animation therefore shows the entire multicolored trajectory with only the camera rotating: animate='window' (documented as 'nothing outside the window is drawn at all') degrades silently into a spin-style animation, and animate=True/parallel with trail flags likewise loses head-window and trails. Probe: the collection holds all 39 segments before and after driving frame 30, and ax.lines is empty for both 'window' and True. Applies to the matplotlib backend (default); the same _apply_multicolor_lines call also handles 2-D (LineCollection).
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
np.random.seed(2)
c = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(200, 6), axis=0)
ha = hyp.plot(c, animate='window', duration=4, frame_rate=10, focused=1, hue=np.arange(200.0), show=False)
ax = ha.figure.axes[0]
print(len(ax.lines))  # 0 -- animated window artists removed
print([len(getattr(a, '_segments3d', [])) for a in ax.collections])  # [39] full trajectory
ha.animation._func(30, *ha.animation._args)
print([len(getattr(a, '_segments3d', [])) for a in ax.collections])  # still 39 full segments
ha.save('hue_window.gif')  # every frame shows the whole rainbow trajectory
findings.expected: The 1-second opaque window slides along the trajectory (11 of 40 interpolated points visible per frame), colored by the hue gradient; nothing outside the window drawn.
findings.actual:
window_frames: 10
lines fargs: ['Line3D']
collection: Line3DCollection nsegs: 39
after frame30 collection nsegs: 39
(ax.lines empty; extracted gif frames f010 and f030 both show the ENTIRE rainbow trajectory, camera rotation only)
animate=True + continuous hue: ax.lines=0

findings.title: animate + legend + any trail flag (chemtrails/precog/bullettime) triples the canvas width; plot squashed into the left third
findings.description: _fit_right_legend (plot.py:3120) iteratively widens the figure until the legend fits, capped at 3.0*w. With an animated 3-D plot that has trail artists (created unclipped via set_clip_on(False) in animate_plot3D), the fit loop runs away and stops at the 3x cap: fig grows 6.4in -> 19.2in wide while the actual content's tight right edge ends at 7.34in, and the function only ever widens (never shrinks back). Every exported frame is a 3840x960 image with the cube+data squashed into the left third and two-thirds dead whitespace. Without a trail flag the same call converges correctly to 7.49in. All three trail flags reproduce it.

findings.title: Multi-dataset animations: frame count driven ONLY by the first dataset -- later datasets that are longer are silently truncated (67% never shown in a 3:1 case)
findings.description: plot.py interpolates every dataset with interp_val computed from xform[0] only (plot.py:2328-2330), and animate_plot3D passes frames=x[0].shape[0] to FuncAnimation (matplotlib_backend.py:1608). With plot([100-row, 300-row], animate=True), the first dataset maps to 40 frames while the longer one needs 121 -- the animation stops at frame 40, so the final two-thirds of the longer dataset are NEVER displayed, with no warning. In the other order ([300, 100]) the shorter dataset simply ends early (consistent row=timepoint semantics) but the truncation direction is silent data loss whose severity depends on argument order. Unequal-length multi-subject recordings are a core hypertools use case.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
np.random.seed(2)
b1 = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(300, 8), axis=0)
b2 = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(100, 8), axis=0)
ha = hyp.plot([b2, b1], animate=True, duration=4, frame_rate=10, show=False)
print(ha.animation._save_count)                      # 40
print([d.shape[0] for d in ha.animation._args[0]])   # [40, 121] -- only first 40 of 121 ever rendered
findings.expected: The animation covers every dataset's full trajectory (e.g. frames = max over datasets, or a documented truncation warning).
findings.actual:
order [100,300]: frames = 40 | interp lengths = [40, 121]
-> longer dataset has 121 interp pts but only 40 frames are shown: fraction shown = 0.33
(order [300,100]: interpolated lengths [40, 14]; final pts per line: [21, 0] -- shorter dataset vanishes for the last two-thirds of the animation)
docs_impact: hypertools/plot/plot.py (animate=True docstring: 'each dataset plotted simultaneously' -- no mention of first-dataset-driven length/truncation)

findings.title: Frame count off by one vs the docstring's 'exactly frame_rate * duration frames' (901/41 instead of 900/40 for some N)
findings.description: For line-styled animations the frame count comes from PCHIP interpolation via np.arange(0, N-1, (N-1)/(frame_rate*duration)) (_shared/helpers.py:139, called from plot.py:2328 with interp_val=frame_rate*duration/(N-1)). Floating-point step error yields one extra sample for some N: N=300 at 30x30 gives 901 frames; N=10/50 at 4x10 give 41. The plot() docstring states 'Both backends generate exactly frame_rate * duration frames'. Consequences are small (one extra frame, ~33ms longer file; a saved 'four-second' gif has 41 frames) but the documented invariant does not hold, and downstream code aligning per-frame annotations to duration*frame_rate would be off by one. np.linspace(0, N-1, round(frame_rate*duration)) would be exact.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np
for N, fr, dur in [(300, 30, 30), (10, 10, 4), (50, 10, 4), (300, 10, 4)]:
    iv = fr * dur / (N - 1)
    print(N, fr, dur, np.arange(0, N - 1, 1 / iv).size, 'target', fr * dur)
# hypertools-level: hyp.plot(np.cumsum(np.random.randn(300,10),axis=0), animate=True, show=False).animation._save_count == 901
findings.expected: Exactly frame_rate * duration frames for every N (900, 40, 40, 40).
findings.actual:
N=300 fr=30 dur=30: arange size=901 target=900
N=10 fr=10 dur=4: arange size=41 target=40
N=50 fr=10 dur=4: arange size=41 target=40
N=300 fr=10 dur=4: arange size=40 target=40

findings.title: Marker-only animations (fmt without a line, e.g. '.') ignore duration/frame_rate pacing: frames = raw row count
findings.description: Interpolation to frame_rate*duration frames is gated on has_line_component(fmt) (plot.py:2326), so a marker-only fmt skips it and FuncAnimation gets frames=x[0].shape[0] = the raw row count. hyp.plot(walk300, '.', animate=True, duration=4, frame_rate=10) produces a 300-frame animation that plays 30 s at fps=10 instead of the requested 4 s -- duration= has no effect at all. Contradicts both the duration docstring ('Length of the animation in seconds') and the frame_rate docstring ('Both backends generate exactly frame_rate * duration frames'), neither of which carves out marker-only styles.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
np.random.seed(1)
walk = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(300, 10), axis=0)
ha = hyp.plot(walk, '.', animate=True, duration=4, frame_rate=10, show=False)
print(ha.animation._save_count)  # 300, not 40 -> saved gif plays 30s, not 4s
findings.expected: 40 frames (4 s at 10 fps), or a documented exception for marker-only animations.

findings.title: animate=2 (truthy non-bool, non-string) silently produces a static plot; with save_path= it crashes with AttributeError on None
findings.description: plot.py's QC fail-fast for unknown animate styles only checks strings (plot.py:1322), and the backend whitelist `animate in [True, 'parallel', ...]` (matplotlib_backend.py:1993) admits 1 (== True) but lets any other truthy scalar fall through to the static branch. So animate=1 animates while animate=2 silently renders static -- and because plot.py's save block does `if animate: _save_animation(line_ani, ...)` with line_ani=None, animate=2 + save_path crashes with a cryptic AttributeError instead of the clear ValueError given for bad strings.

hyp.plot(w, animate=2, save_path='/tmp/an2.gif', show=False)  # AttributeError

findings.title: GIF exports at the default frame_rate=30 play ~10% fast (27.0s for a requested 30s): 33ms delay rounds to GIF's 30ms centisecond grid
findings.description: PillowWriter receives fps=frame_rate and writes per-frame duration int(1000/30)=33ms, which the GIF format stores in centiseconds -> 30ms/frame. A default-parameters animation (900 frames) therefore has wall-clock 27.0s instead of 30s; the requested duration=1s at fr=30 measures 0.900s. animate.py's comment block (lines 22-27) says an exported file 'plays in real time: ... total ~= duration seconds'. mp4 exports are exact (60 frames / 2.000000s at fr=30), and frame rates whose period is a multiple of 10ms (10, 12.5, 20, 25, 50) are exact in GIF too. Worth either defaulting GIFs to a centisecond-friendly effective fps or documenting the format limitation.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
from PIL import Image, ImageSequence
w = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(300, 10), axis=0)
ha = hyp.plot(w, animate='window', duration=1, frame_rate=30, focused=0.2, show=False)
ha.save('/tmp/d1fr30.gif')
im = Image.open('/tmp/d1fr30.gif')
durs = [f.info.get('duration') for f in ImageSequence.Iterator(im)]

findings.title: Saving to an unknown/missing extension raises a raw ffmpeg CalledProcessError (leaked command line) instead of naming supported formats
findings.description: _save_animation (animate.py:28-47) routes any extension it does not recognize -- including a path with NO extension at all, since rsplit('.', 1)[-1] returns the whole basename -- to the ffmpeg writer. ffmpeg then fails and matplotlib surfaces subprocess.CalledProcessError whose message is the full 20-argument ffmpeg command line; the helpful hint ('use a standard extension for the filename') only appears in a separately-printed MovieWriter stderr log. A user typo like anim.saev -> anim.xyz or a missing extension gets an intimidating traceback instead of 'unsupported extension .xyz; supported: .gif, .png/.apng, .svg, .mp4/.mov/.avi (ffmpeg formats)'.
findings.repro:
import numpy as np, hypertools as hyp
w = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(60, 5), axis=0)
ha = hyp.plot(w, animate='window', duration=1, frame_rate=5, show=False)
ha.save('/tmp/anim.xyz')
findings.expected: ValueError naming the unsupported extension and the supported ones.
findings.actual: RAISED CalledProcessError: Command '['ffmpeg', '-f', 'rawvideo', '-vcodec', 'rawvideo', '-s', '1280x960', '-pix_fmt', 'rgba', '-framerate', '5', '-loglevel', 'error', '-i', 'pipe:', '-vcodec', 'h264', ...]' (MovieWriter stderr: Unable to choose an output format for '.../anim.xyz'; use a standard extension for the filename or specify the format manually.)

findings.title: 1-D + animate rejects via bare `assert` (AssertionError) instead of the ValueError used by every sibling animate validation; first window/parallel frame is an empty cube
findings.description: (a) matplotlib_backend.py:1998 guards 2-D/3-D-only animation with `assert x[0].shape[1] in (2, 3)` -- the message is good, but it surfaces as AssertionError (inconsistent with the ValueErrors raised for every other invalid animate input) and disappears under `python -O`. (b) Cosmetic: frame 0 of window/parallel animations draws a single-point line window -- invisible for line fmts -- so exported files open on an empty cube for 1/frame_rate seconds (see window3d_frame000.png); seeding the first window with 2 points would avoid the blank opening frame.
